definition.text: An economy or market is efficient when it gets the most of what people want, such as well-being, out of the resources it has; economists usually mean allocative (Pareto) or productive efficiency.

facts.text: Allocative or Pareto efficiency means no change could help one person without harming another; productive efficiency means no more of one good can be made without making less of another, at the lowest average cost.
The two ideas are not the same: a market can be allocatively efficient without being productively efficient, or the other way round.
Because productive resources are scarce, they must go to each industry in just the right amounts, or too much or too little gets produced.
One school of thought stresses the distortions that governments create; another stresses the distortions that markets create and wants more government involvement to fix them.
The first welfare theorem says a perfectly competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient, but this only holds without market imperfections, which are significant in real markets.
Efficiency in the Pareto sense says nothing about equality or the overall well-being of a society.
Removing one market distortion does not always raise efficiency: if another distortion cannot be removed, the theory of the second best says efficiency may even fall.
Many economists consider carbon pricing the most economically efficient way to cut greenhouse gas emissions.

definition.text: The branch of economics that uses the tools of microeconomics to judge how well off a society is as a whole.

facts.text: Welfare economics guides public economics, which studies how government action can improve social welfare, and it is the theoretical basis of cost–benefit analysis.
Its first fundamental theorem says competitive markets, under certain assumptions, give Pareto efficient outcomes, an idea sometimes linked to Adam Smith's invisible hand.
Its second theorem says any Pareto efficient outcome can be reached through a competitive market if a planner first makes lump-sum transfers.
Arrow's impossibility theorem is sometimes counted as a third fundamental theorem of welfare economics.
The early neoclassical approach was built by Edgeworth, Sidgwick, Marshall and Pigou; the later 'new welfare economics' rests on the work of Pareto, Kaldor, Hicks and Scitovsky.
The idea of an externality, developed by Pigou, remains central to modern welfare economics and to environmental economics.
Amartya Sen urged welfare research to use a wider range of data and to discuss ethics and morality openly.
Austrian school economists reject both cardinal and ordinal welfare economics because they rely on comparing different people's utility.

definition.text: A rule that ranks possible states of society from more to less desirable by combining the preferences of everyone in it.

facts.text: Economists use social welfare functions to decide which of two outcomes, such as two income distributions, is better for society as a whole.
Unlike one consumer's utility function, it maps many people's utility functions onto a single result.
Ordinal versions use only whether one option is better than another; cardinal versions also use how much better it is.
Abram Bergson introduced the term in a 1938 article to state precisely the value judgements needed to define maximum economic welfare.
In 1935 Lionel Robbins argued that changes in different people's utilities cannot be compared by any empirical test.
Arrow's impossibility theorem shows that, unlike a single consumer, a society cannot build a fully consistent decision rule from ranked preferences alone.

definition.text: A social welfare function that takes numerical measures of each person's well-being, often income, and turns them into one number for the whole society's welfare.

facts.text: The utilitarian or Benthamite version adds up individual utilities, so it maximizes total income without caring how that income is shared.
Under the utilitarian version, society should accept a transfer from poor to rich if the rich gain more utility than the poor lose.
The max-min or Rawlsian version, based on John Rawls, judges society by the welfare of its worst-off member alone.
The max-min function can be read as society showing an extreme aversion to uncertainty, caring only about the worst position anyone could face.
In 1973 Amartya Sen proposed a welfare function equal to average income multiplied by one minus the Gini index.

definition.text: The result that if society's choices follow the rules of rational choice under risk, the social welfare function must be the utilitarian sum of individual utilities.

facts.text: By the theorem, any non-utilitarian rule is incoherent: it will accept some bets that every member of society opposes.
With a weaker condition, that rankings do not depend on the unit (cents or dollars), the welfare function must belong to the isoelastic family.
In that family, one parameter value gives the Nash bargaining solution (maximizing the product of utilities) and another gives the utilitarian sum.
Requiring the Pigou–Dalton principle, that inequality is not a good thing, limits the parameter to at most 1.

definition.text: The four marginal conditions on consumption and production that must all hold for an economy to be Pareto efficient.

facts.text: Every consumer must have the same marginal rate of substitution between any two goods, so no swap between consumers can make both happier.
Every producer must have the same marginal rate of transformation between two goods, so shifting production between producers cannot raise total output.
A factor such as labour must have the same marginal product at every producer of a good, so moving production cannot cut its cost.
Consumers' marginal rates of substitution must equal producers' marginal rates of transformation, so changing the product mix cannot make consumers happier.

definition.text: The conditions, such as monopoly, hidden information or poorly designed regulation, that keep an economy from reaching Pareto efficiency.

facts.text: Imperfect market structures such as monopoly, monopsony, oligopoly and monopolistic competition cause inefficiency.
Asymmetric information, including principal–agent problems, and the falling long-run costs of a natural monopoly also cause inefficiency.
Government limits on prices and quantities and other regulation arising from government failure can also make an economy inefficient.
One inefficiency can offset another: if pollution leads to too many tyres being made, a tax on tyres might restore the efficient amount.

definition.text: The conflict that arises because policies making the economy fairer usually cost some efficiency, so society must choose between the two.

facts.text: Redistributing income is costly, so there is a built-in choice between more efficiency and more equity.
Much economic research therefore measures the efficiency losses of tax and transfer programmes, which redistribute by their nature.
The trade-off is at the heart of many debates about tax policy; its formal study was begun by James Mirrlees in 1971.
Because real markets are imperfect, emissions trading may also involve a trade-off between equity and efficiency.

definition.text: The early neoclassical approach to welfare, built by Edgeworth, Sidgwick, Marshall and Pigou, which treated utility as measurable and added it up across people.

facts.text: It assumed utility can be measured on a scale, that preferences are fixed and stable, and that each extra unit consumed adds less and less utility.
With those assumptions a social welfare function is simply the sum of all individual utility functions, in the tradition of Bentham.
It was often inferred that moving income from a rich person to a poor person tends to raise total utility.

definition.text: The ordinal approach to welfare, based on the work of Pareto, Kaldor, Hicks and Scitovsky, which judges efficiency without measuring or comparing people's utility.

facts.text: It treats efficiency and distribution separately: efficiency is judged by Pareto and Kaldor–Hicks criteria, distribution by the choice of social welfare function.
It replaces measurable utility with ordinal utility, which only ranks bundles of goods, for example on an indifference-curve map.
The consensus behind it largely collapsed after Arrow's impossibility theorem and utility representation theorems showed such approaches to be self-contradictory.
Murray Rothbard proposed rebuilding welfare economics on 'demonstrated preference', under which only voluntary market exchanges clearly raise welfare.
